briefing.text: Lesion type is not a clinical column: CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED reads 'Invasive Breast Carcinoma' for every sample, including JP and DCIS. Take lesion type from the SAMPLE_ID suffix (-JP, -DCIS, -IDC). Only patient JuP3 has a matched JP, DCIS and IDC. JuP1 and JuP2 have one unsuffixed sample each. The hypothesis is about JP versus its associated DCIS and IDC, so the main comparison is within JuP3 (JuP3-JP vs JuP3-DCIS vs JuP3-IDC). Do not pool the unmatched samples into a JP group, and state that one matched trio supports only a descriptive comparison.
briefing.reason: Grouping by the clinical column or pooling unmatched samples would give the wrong comparison.

briefing.text: data_cna_hg19.seg contains segmented copy number for JuP3-JP, JuP3-DCIS and JuP3-IDC (and for JuP1 and JuP2), so CNA burden per lesion can be computed. The relevant variable therefore exists. If JP shows fewer or similar CNAs than its matched DCIS/IDC, that counts as evidence against the hypothesis, not as grounds for 'Not verifiable'.
briefing.reason: This prevents a wrong 'Not verifiable' label and clarifies what counts as contrary evidence.

briefing.text: Counting raw .seg rows measures segmentation, not alterations, and many segments may be copy-neutral. For each sample, compute (a) the number of segments, (b) the number of segments with |seg.mean| above a threshold, and (c) the fraction of genome altered (bp with |seg.mean| > threshold divided by total bp). Also tabulate num.mark and segment length, and recount after excluding small or low-marker segments (e.g. num.mark<10 or <1 Mb). Base the conclusion on called alterations, and report it as metric-dependent if the metrics disagree on direction.
briefing.reason: The choice of CNA burden metric and noise filtering can decide the direction of the comparison.

briefing.text: CNA calls from log2 seg.mean depend on the threshold (cBioPortal FGA uses 0.1, CNVkit uses gain>0.2 and loss<-0.25, others use ±0.3). Recompute thresholded counts and FGA at 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3, plus high-level cutoffs, for the three JuP3 lesions. Check whether the JP vs DCIS/IDC ordering holds across thresholds, and say so explicitly if it flips.
briefing.reason: The ranking may change with the cutoff, which affects how confident a True/False call can be.

briefing.text: Check each sample's length-weighted median seg.mean. It should be near 0. If it is not, recentre by subtracting it before thresholding, and report whether the conclusions change.
briefing.reason: A shifted baseline can create or erase apparent genome-wide alterations in one lesion.

briefing.text: No tumour purity values are provided. Normal-cell contamination pulls log2 ratios toward 0, so a lower-cellularity lesion can show fewer events above a fixed threshold. Compare the per-sample |seg.mean| distribution (max, 95th percentile) and check whether the same loci are altered at different amplitudes across the lesions. Note this limitation in the reasoning, but still report the observed burden.
briefing.reason: Without this check, amplitude differences could be misread as differences in the number of alterations.

shared_assumptions: Both teams treat 'number of copy number alterations' as a burden measure (fraction genome altered and thresholded segment counts) and judge mainly by FGA or high-threshold counts. Neither team fixed one primary metric in advance that matches the wording 'number of CNAs'.

Both treat the single matched JuP3 trio as the test and assume the three samples' seg.mean values sit on one comparable scale (same baseline, same tumour content). No purity or ploidy estimate exists to support that.

Both assume that a low-amplitude JP profile means few alterations and not a diluted signal. Team A's argument from absent shared arm events depends on the JP sharing clonal events with the DCIS/IDC, which is itself unproven.
Both assume the lesion type of JuP1 and JuP2 (no suffix, labelled 'Invasive Breast Carcinoma' like every sample) is JP. Team B uses them as JP context without testing that.
unused_evidence: data_mutations.txt: neither team used variant allele fractions (t_alt_count/t_ref_count) to estimate the relative tumour content of JuP3-JP vs DCIS vs IDC. That is the only purity proxy in the data, and it bears directly on whether JP CNAs are attenuated.

TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS in the sample table (JP 0.1 vs DCIS 1.4, IDC 1.17) and shared mutations across the trio: these would show whether the JP is clonally related to the DCIS/IDC and whether its low signal fits low cellularity.
num.mark per segment, which shows how well each JP segment is supported. Team B did not filter small or low-marker segments, and its altered-segment counts may include noise.
Raw segment counts per sample (JP 48, DCIS 54, IDC 49; JuP1 36, JuP2 37). Neither team reported them as one reading of 'number of CNAs'.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named low JP purity as their weakest point. Neither resolved it: team A reported max |seg.mean| of 0.21 for JP and argued from the absence of shared events, and team B only stated the concern. Neither used a VAF-based purity proxy.

Team A found that the JP count at |0.1| (18) equals the DCIS count (18) and exceeds the IDC count (17). That means the direction depends on the metric. Team A put the conclusion on FGA without explaining why a count-based reading of 'number' should be set aside.
n=1 matched trio. Neither team said how a single-patient descriptive difference maps onto the True / False / Not verifiable label rules.
second_readings: 'High number of CNAs' could mean the count of CNA events or segments, not the fraction of genome altered. At |0.1| the JP count ties DCIS and exceeds IDC.
'High' could be absolute, meaning JP lesions carry many CNAs for a benign or precursor lesion, with DCIS/IDC only as a reference. The reading 'higher than DCIS and IDC' is the other option.
'JP' could refer to all JP samples (JuP1, JuP2, JuP3-JP), with 'associated DCIS and IDC-NST' as the JuP3 lesions, not only the JuP3 within-patient comparison.
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust. On FGA and high-threshold calls the data point the same way for both teams. But the evidence is one trio, the count-based reading of 'number of CNAs' gives a tie at the lowest threshold, and the low-purity explanation for the flat JP profile was named by both teams and resolved by neither, even though VAFs in the mutation file could test it.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your |0.1| altered-segment count puts JP (18) level with DCIS (18) and above IDC (17). Tabulate raw segment counts and thresholded counts after your num.mark/length filter, side by side with FGA, for each JuP3 lesion. If 'number of CNAs' is read as a count of events, does the direction of your conclusion still hold? If not, does that change the method or the label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Use t_alt_count and t_ref_count in data_mutations.txt to compute the VAF distribution of the JuP3-JP, JuP3-DCIS and JuP3-IDC mutations as a relative tumour-content proxy. If the JP VAFs are much lower, is low cellularity rather than few CNAs the simpler explanation for the flat JP profile, and does that change the method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your purity argument relies on DCIS/IDC arm events being absent in JP, not attenuated. Check in data_mutations.txt whether JuP3-JP shares any mutations (same position and allele) with JuP3-DCIS or JuP3-IDC. If none are shared, the JP may not be clonally related, and absent shared events says nothing about purity. Does that change how you weigh this check?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Compute the same CNA metrics for JuP1 and JuP2 and compare them with JuP3-JP. If those samples are JP lesions, do they show the same low-burden pattern, or does JuP3-JP look like an outlier (for example a low-cellularity sample)? Does the result change whether you keep the comparison within JuP3 only?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your altered-segment counts did not exclude small or low-marker segments. Recount after removing segments with low num.mark or short length, and also report raw segment counts per lesion. Does JP's position relative to DCIS and IDC change under any count-based metric, and does that change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You named low JP purity as your weakest point but did not test it. Compute the VAF distribution per JuP3 lesion from t_alt_count/t_ref_count in data_mutations.txt. If JuP3-JP VAFs are clearly lower, does that weaken the inference that JP has fewer CNAs, and how does it bear on choosing between False and Not verifiable?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You used JuP1 and JuP2 as JP context, but every sample's clinical label reads 'Invasive Breast Carcinoma' and those two IDs have no lesion suffix. What evidence in the data shows they are JP lesions? If none does, does excluding them change your reasoning?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Check whether JuP3-JP shares any somatic mutations (same position and allele) with JuP3-DCIS or JuP3-IDC in data_mutations.txt. Whether the JP is clonally related bears on whether 'associated' lesions are a fair within-patient comparison. Does the result change how you frame the comparison?

How is tumour purity or relative tumour content usually estimated from somatic variant allele fractions in whole-exome data when no matched purity tool output is available, and how strongly does low purity shrink log2 segment means and reduce copy-number calls?
questions.why: Both teams' weakest point is possible low purity in the precursor lesion. Neither showed how to test it or how far it could hide CNAs.

questions.question: In cancer-genomics literature, when a study reports that a lesion has a 'high number of copy number alterations', is that usually measured as a count of CNA segments or events, or as fraction of genome altered, and what log2 thresholds are conventional?
questions.why: The teams' metrics disagree at the lowest threshold. Which metric the claim refers to decides how to read a tie or split.

findings.question: How is tumour purity or relative tumour content usually estimated from somatic variant allele fractions in whole-exome data when no matched purity tool output is available, and how strongly does low purity shrink log2 segment means and reduce copy-number calls?
findings.answer: Purity is estimated as about 2x the VAF of clonal, heterozygous (monoallelic) somatic SNVs in copy-neutral regions, because these centre at VAF 0.5 in a pure tumour. TPES computes purity as observed VAF divided by expected VAF, using only SNVs in segments with log2R in [-0.1, 0.1]. PurityEst uses the mutant allele fraction at heterozygous somatic loci, averaged robustly per chromosome. CNVkit's documentation says the VAF of a clonal driver indicates purity. Copy-number changes at a mutated site and subclonality bias the estimate, so the median or upper mode of VAFs in neutral segments is preferred. Normal-cell contamination dilutes the copy ratio to (1 - p) + p*CN/2. A clonal single-copy loss is log2 -1.0 at 100% purity and -0.415 at 50% (CNVkit's worked example). A single-copy gain is 0.585 at 100% purity. The remaining values below come from applying the same formula: a gain is about 0.32 at 50%, about 0.20 at 30% and about 0.14 at 20%; a loss is about -0.23 at 30% and -0.15 at 20%. So below roughly 30% purity, clonal single-copy events fall at or under the common |log2| > 0.2 cutoff. Low purity can therefore greatly reduce both event counts and FGA, and can hide CNAs in a low-purity precursor lesion.

findings.question: In cancer-genomics literature, when a study reports that a lesion has a 'high number of copy number alterations', is that usually measured as a count of CNA segments or events, or as fraction of genome altered, and what log2 thresholds are conventional?
findings.answer: Both measures are used, and the web does not settle which one a given claim means. One is a count of altered segments or events (segments with |log2| above a cutoff). The other is fraction of genome altered (FGA): the summed length of segments with |log2| above a cutoff divided by the length of all measured segments. FGA is cBioPortal's standard summary. 'High number of CNAs' literally reads as a count of events, but that is an inference about wording, not a documented convention. On cutoffs, |log2| > 0.2 is described as the conventional one for FGA. cBioPortal staff gave 0.1 in one help post and 0.2 in another. A cutoff of 0.1 is used as a lenient alternative (Spurr et al.'s AS/FGA), and CNVkit suggests 0.1-0.3 for gene-level calls. CNVkit's default call thresholds are -1.1, -0.25, 0.2 and 0.7. A comparison that holds only at the most lenient cutoff, or only with one metric, is weak evidence.
